title: Cause of Friction (part 1)
textbookText: Fig 4.9 (a): Showing Frictional Phenomena Cause of Friction In the intricate interplay of interacting surfaces, frictional force materializes as a consequence of the microscopic interactions between atoms and molecules at the point of contact. This force acts tangentially to the direction of motion, creating a resistance that impedes the smooth glide of one surface over the other. The cause of how friction arises is described in the following two ways: viii) Modern Approach: The phenomenon of adhesion between two solid surfaces due to the molecular attraction of the molecules present on the solid surface is the cause of arising friction. 4.7 Types of Friction:
Static and Kinetic Friction Activity 4.4 Do the activities that follow:

Place a heavy mass on a horizontal surface. ix) Try to slowly pull or push the object. x) Seek assistance from your friend and attempt the same on the object; however, you still observe no movement in the object. xi) Continue by adding more friends—one, two, three, and so on—and have them participate in the same activity. Eventually, the object reaches a state where it begins to move over the ground xii) After moving, remove one, two, or more friends, but the body continues to move.
- Why were so many people involved in moving the body? - Why does the motion continue even after removing one or two people once the body is in motion?

Before initiating motion, there exists the frictional force between the body and the ground surface. This type of friction, occurring between the bodies before they come into motion, is referred to as static friction Physics, Grade 11 | 91

More clearly, to say, static friction is the friction between the solids in contact but at rest. As we continue to apply additional force to pull the body, the cumulative force endeavors to overcome static friction, allowing the body to initiate movement over the surface The maximum value of the frictional force a body just begins to move over the other body is called limiting friction. This force reaches its maximum value. After the body is in motion, there is no need of such a great force as the body has been set into motion from the rest, and the body continues its motion even with a lesser force. Hence the friction between two solids during the motion is called kinetic (or dynamic) friction. And, Static friction > Kinetic friction.

Fig 4.9 (b): Showing Frictional Phenomena Sliding and Rolling Friction The phenomenon of arising a counteracting force when a body is sliding over another solid surface is called sliding friction. In the same way, the phenomenon of arising a resisting force between two solids when one body is rolling over the surface is called rolling friction. These distinct forms of friction elucidate the dynamic interactions between surfaces in different modes of motion, offering insights into the diverse forces at play in the realm of mechanical interactions. 4.8 Law of Friction Followings are the laws: i) The phenomenon of friction between two surfaces opposes the relative motion between the surfaces. ii) The friction depends up on the roughness of the surface. iii) The frictional force acts parallel to the surface in touch iv) The friction is independent on the area of the surface in touch. v) The kinetic friction is independent of the relative velocities of the surfaces. vi) The magnitude of the frictional force is directly proportional to the normal reaction i.e. F ∝ R. Physics, Grade 11 | 92
∴ F = μR Here, μ = F/R is called the coefficient of friction.

For static friction, μs = F/R and for kinetic (dynamic) friction, μk =F/R And μs > μk Friction is a necessary evil. Justify your answer. Friction is necessary to us for walking, putting a nail on a wall, writing on a piece of paper, driving and stopping a vehicle, and in so many phenomena. In every observed phenomenon, the presence of friction leads to energy loss, as it staunchly opposes the motion of objects and contributes to wear and tear. Consequently, the efficiency of the system diminishes, never reaching the ideal 100%. This consistent interplay between friction, energy dissipation, and reduced efficiency underscores the real-world challenges in achieving perfect mechanical performance across various processes and systems. Hence, friction is necessary in so many events, but due to energy loss, it appears as an evil. Some Facts: a. To show limiting friction is directly proportional to the normal reaction (F ∝ R):
